comment_data.body:
I am not sure which platforms actually use the CSPRNG, since it is only used as a fallback.

Linux uses the getrandom syscall, fallsback to /dev/random (or /dev/urandom)
Windows uses the RtlGenRandom syscall, which we dont know the details off, but on wine this falls back to /dev/random (or 0 if those devices dont exist) and on reactos they use a LCG with current time, which they even say is absolutely not usable for crypto.
Not sure about other platform.

comment_data.body:
getrandom:
> These bytes can be used to seed user-space random number generators or for cryptographic purposes.

If it can be used for cryptographic purposes, I think it can be considered a CSPRNG.

/dev/random:
> In Unix-like operating systems, /dev/random and /dev/urandom are special files that serve as cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generators (CSPRNGs).

Windows: ack.

Ultimately though, for this comment it doesn't matter, because libsodium claims it's a CSPRNG, so it is. If it's not, it's a libsodium bug and you should file one. From libsodium docs:
> The library provides a set of functions to generate unpredictable data, suitable for creating secret keys.
